source_refs.note: Topic 1.7.4, printed pages 11-12: the definitions of first and second electron affinity, the oxide-ion example and the factors.

blocks.title: First electron affinity
blocks.text: The first electron affinity (delta H ea1) is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous uni-negative ions under standard conditions.

For chlorine, Cl(g) + e- gives Cl-(g), delta H ea1 = -348.8 kJ per mol: the energy released when 6.02 x 10 to the power 23 chlorine atoms in the gaseous state become chloride ions. Since energy is released, the first electron affinity carries a negative sign. The second electron affinity (delta H ea2) is the energy required to add electrons to 1 mole of uni-negative gaseous ions to form 1 mole of gaseous 2- ions under standard conditions. When a first electron is added to a neutral oxygen atom, 141 kJ per mol is released: O(g) + e- gives O-(g), delta H ea1 = -141 kJ per mol. But 798 kJ per mol is absorbed on adding a second electron to the uni-negative ion: O-(g) + e- gives O2-(g), delta H ea2 = +798 kJ per mol. The net enthalpy change for forming the oxide ion is the sum: O(g) + 2e- gives O2-(g), (-141) + (+798) = +657 kJ per mol.

items: Size of the atom: for small atoms the attraction of the nucleus for the incoming electron is stronger, so the smaller the atom, the greater its electron affinity.
Nuclear charge: the greater the nuclear charge, the stronger the attraction for the incoming electron, so electron affinity rises with nuclear charge.

Electronic configuration: the electron affinity is low when the electron is added to a half-filled subshell. The group 15 atoms nitrogen and phosphorus (N = 2s2 2p3, P = 3s2 3p3) have very low values because their stable half-filled p subshells have little tendency to accept an extra electron. The noble gases of group 18, with stable ns2 np6 configurations, do not accept an extra electron, as their positive first electron affinities show.
